680.title: Passover: it would have been enough
680.hook: a song counting gifts one by one
680.tomorrow: Passover: as if you left (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)
680.howItsDone: At the seder, after the telling of the plagues, families sing Dayenu together, with everyone joining the chorus; in some Persian and Afghan Jewish homes, people playfully tap each other with scallions during the song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four children, and the one who doesn't know how to ask. Your line was answer each child. Today, a song the whole table shouts.

Partway through the seder, after a long stretch of reading, the energy changes. Someone starts a song with a three-syllable chorus, and suddenly everyone, the uncle checking his phone, the toddler under the table, is shouting it. Day, day, enu. Day, day, enu. In some Persian and Afghan Jewish families, people grab scallions and playfully swat each other during the chorus, recalling the whips of slavery. It can get rowdy. And underneath the noise, the song is doing something careful: counting.
screen: `THE ENERGY CHANGES.` → `SCALLIONS IN THE AIR.` → `UNDERNEATH: COUNTING.`

segments.voice: Dayenu means it would have been enough for us. The song walks through the Exodus in fifteen steps, each one a gift. If God had brought us out of Egypt, and not brought judgment on the Egyptians: dayenu. If God had split the sea, and not led us through on dry ground: dayenu. If God had fed us manna, and not given us Shabbat. If God had brought us to Mount Sinai, and not given us the Torah. All the way to the land of Israel and the Temple. Fifteen times the table shouts: that would have been enough. The Haggadah introduces it with a line: how many good steps God has done for us. The full song appears in an early prayer order compiled in Babylonia by a scholar named Amram Gaon. Some lines sound strange taken literally. Would standing at Sinai without the Torah really have been enough? Teachers have answered in different ways. One answer: the song isn't making a claim about history. It's training the eye. Each step deserved a whole thank-you of its own, so don't let the gifts blur into one lump. Then the Haggadah turns it around: how much more should we be grateful, since God did all of them. It's easy to give thanks in bulk. Dayenu gives thanks one gift at a time.

segments.voice: Think of one good thing in your life, maybe a person, and break it into steps: if they had only shown up once, enough; if they had only stayed, enough. Go slowly, one gift at a time, saying dayenu after each, out loud or in your head.
Dayenu. It would have been enough for us: the seder's song of fifteen gifts, counted one by one. Today's word.
Your line: it would have been enough. Fifteen gifts, each one counted on its own. Until tomorrow.

681.title: Passover: as if you left (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)
681.hook: in every generation each person must see themselves as if they left Egypt
681.howItsDone: At the seder, the Haggadah reads the Mishnah's line that in every generation each person must see themselves as if they left Egypt; people recline and drink four cups as free people, and then sing the Psalms of Hallel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dayenu, fifteen gifts counted one by one. Your line was it would have been enough. Today, the line that makes the whole seder personal.

An anniversary looks back. A national holiday remembers founders long gone. You honor them, but you weren't there. The seder could work the same way: here's what happened to our ancestors, pass the matzah. But a sentence in the Mishnah, read aloud at the seder, refuses to let the story stay in the past tense. It doesn't ask you to remember the Exodus. It asks for something much stranger.
screen: `ANNIVERSARIES LOOK BACK.` → `YOU WEREN'T THERE.` → `A SENTENCE THAT REFUSES.`

segments.voice: At the end of the tractate on Passover, the Mishnah gives Rabban Gamliel's rule: whoever hasn't explained three things at the seder, the Passover offering, matzah and bitter herbs, hasn't fulfilled the duty of the night. Then: in every generation, a person is obligated to see himself as if he himself came out of Egypt. Not our ancestors. Me. The proof is the verse from two days ago, in the old Jewish translation: "It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." The verse speaks in the first person to people who were never slaves. Maimonides, in his version of this law, uses a slightly different word: a person must show himself as if he left. Show, not just see. That's why, he says, people recline at the seder, like free people at a banquet, and drink the cups. The body acts it out. And the Mishnah draws a conclusion: because we came out, we're obligated to thank and praise God. Then the seder breaks into the Psalms of praise. Remembering turns into gratitude, and gratitude into song. One more layer, a wordplay Hasidic teachers used. The Hebrew name for Egypt, Mitzrayim, sounds like meitzarim: narrow places, tight straits. So every person, they taught, has an Egypt, a narrow place they've been held. The seder asks each one to stand in the doorway of their own leaving, every year.

segments.voice: Sit back, the way someone free would sit, and think of a narrow place you've been in: a job, an illness, a fear, a season when the walls felt close. Picture the moment you stepped out, or the step you hope to take, and let your shoulders open. You don't have to be fully out; just stand in the doorway for a moment, as if you left.
Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, told in the first person, as if you yourself left. Today's word.
Your line: as if you left. The story is told in the first person, every year. See you tomorrow.

682.title: Passover: Elijah's cup
682.hook: a cup is poured for Elijah and the door is opened
682.howItsDone: Near the end of the seder, after grace after meals, families fill a cup for Elijah and open the front door while reciting 'Pour out Your wrath' from the Psalms; some families now also place a cup of water for Miriam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah's in every generation. Your line was as if you left. Tonight, someone else is expected at the table.

It's late. The meal is over, grace after meals is said, and the children are fading. Then someone fills a large, often beautiful cup that's sat untouched all night. A child is sent to open the front door, and cold air comes in. Everyone stands, or goes quiet, or sings. The youngest kids watch the cup closely, certain that if they look hard enough, they'll see the wine go down a little. Nobody invited this guest. He's been expected for a very long time.
screen: `A CUP UNTOUCHED ALL NIGHT.` → `A CHILD OPENS THE DOOR.` → `WATCHING THE WINE.`

segments.voice: The guest is Elijah, the prophet. In the book of Kings, the text never says he dies; he's carried up to heaven in a whirlwind, with a chariot of fire. So in Jewish tradition, he never quite left. He turns up in Talmudic stories disguised as a traveler, a beggar, a merchant. And Malachi, whose book closes the Prophets, ends with a promise: God will send Elijah before the great day of the LORD. In the old Jewish translation: "And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." So Elijah became the messenger of redemption. Why a cup? Are there four cups at the seder, or five? Some versions of the Talmud mention a fifth. A popular later explanation says that since the question was never settled, a fifth cup is poured, not drunk, and named for Elijah, who, tradition says, will one day answer the questions the rabbis left open. Why open the door? It's opened right before a passage asking God to pour out wrath on the nations that devoured Israel, words from the Psalms, said in years of real persecution. The Torah calls this night a night of watching, so some explain there's nothing to fear in opening the door. And Elijah, if he's coming, should find it open. More recently, some families add a cup of water for Miriam, the prophet, beside Elijah's; others keep the older custom alone. Either way, the seder ends with the door open, waiting.

segments.voice: If you can, open a door or a window and feel the air change. Think of what you're waiting for: a reconciliation, a recovery, a turn in the world, a guest you haven't met yet. Malachi's promise was about hearts turning toward each other, so stay with one heart you'd like turned toward you, or yours toward them.
Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, and a night that ends with Elijah's cup poured and the door left open. Today's word.
Your line: leave the door open. In Jewish tradition, Elijah is still expected. Day six hundred eighty-two, done.

683.title: Passover: the Song of Songs
683.hook: a love poem read at Passover, which the rabbis read as God and Israel
683.tomorrow: The Omer: one quality a day
683.howItsDone: Many Ashkenazi synagogues read the Song of Songs aloud on the Shabbat during Passover, and some Sephardi and Mizrahi communities also chant it every Friday evening before Shabbat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elijah's cup and the open door. Your line was leave the door open. Today, the book read in the week of Passover.

A love poem, of all things, in the Bible. Not a gentle one, either. Two lovers searching for each other through city streets at night. Eyes like doves, hair like a flock of goats coming down a mountain. Kisses, perfume, a garden locked and then opened, a watchman in the streets. Nowhere in its eight chapters does God's name clearly appear. And during the week of Passover, it's the custom in synagogue to read it aloud, beginning to end.
screen: `A LOVE POEM IN A HOLY BOOK.` → `EYES LIKE DOVES.` → `READ ALOUD AT PASSOVER.`

segments.voice: It's called Shir HaShirim, the Song of Songs, meaning the greatest song, the way holy of holies means the holiest place. The rabbis of the Mishnah debated which books belonged in the Bible, and some doubted this one. Rabbi Akiva answered: all the writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies. He and the rabbis after him read it as a love song between God and the people Israel. The ancient Aramaic translation, the Targum, goes further and reads it as Israel's history, starting with the Exodus. So why Passover? The plainest reason is the season. In the old Jewish translation, the beloved calls: "For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; the flowers appear on the earth; the time of singing is come." Passover is the spring festival, and this is a spring poem. The deeper reason is the story. In the rabbis' reading, the Exodus begins the romance: God takes Israel out of Egypt into the wilderness, like a bride following her beloved. For some readers, one verse sums it up: "My beloved is mine, and I am his." Among Ashkenazim, it's usually read on the Shabbat during the festival; some Sephardi communities also chant it every Friday evening, as Shabbat comes in. Read as a love poem, it's beautiful. Read the rabbis' way, as a parable, it pictures the bond between God and Israel as longing, on both sides.

Then sit with whoever it makes you think of: a partner, a parent, a child, a friend, or, if you pray, God. Let the longing in it be good rather than sad.

684.title: The Omer: one quality a day
684.hook: the mystics pair each of the forty-nine days with a quality to refine
684.howItsDone: From the second night of Passover until Shavuot, observant Jews count the Omer each evening with a blessing, naming the day and week; many also follow the Kabbalistic chart of sefirot, reflecting on one quality each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of Songs, read in the week of Passover. Your line was the song of songs. Today, the seven weeks from Passover to Shavuot.

Every evening for seven weeks, after nightfall, observant Jews say a blessing and then a number. Today is one day of the Omer. Today is two days. Today is eight days, which is one week and one day. Miss a whole day, and by many rulings you keep counting but stop saying the blessing. Apps, wall charts and little fridge calendars help people keep track. It sounds like the world's most patient countdown. But the mystics turned these forty-nine days into something closer to a training plan.
screen: `A BLESSING, THEN A NUMBER.` → `FORTY-NINE NIGHTS.` → `A COUNTDOWN, OR A TRAINING PLAN?`

segments.voice: Start with the Torah. In Leviticus, from the day the first sheaf of barley is brought, the omer, you count. In the old Jewish translation: "seven weeks shall there be complete." On the fiftieth day comes Shavuot, the feast of weeks. In the rabbis' reading, it's the road from leaving Egypt to receiving the Torah at Sinai: freedom first, then what to do with it. The word for counting is sefirah, and here the mystics come in. In the Kabbalah, a very similar word, sefirot, names the qualities through which God is revealed in the world. The lower seven are usually listed as chesed, loving-kindness; gevurah, strength or restraint; tiferet, beauty and balance; netzach, endurance; hod, humility or splendor; yesod, foundation, the bond between people; and malchut, kingship, presence, the way it all shows up in the world. Seven qualities, seven weeks, and inside each week, seven days. So the first day is loving-kindness within loving-kindness. The second, strength within loving-kindness: love that knows its limits. Forty-nine combinations, one each night. Kabbalists and Hasidic teachers built a practice on it, and many teachers of character, middot, still use it: each day, look at one quality in yourself and refine it a little. Just today's square on the chart. The counting stops being a wait and becomes the preparation. By the time you reach the mountain, you've worked on the person who's arriving.

segments.voice: Choose one quality: kindness, restraint, balance, endurance, humility, connection or presence, maybe the one that's been weakest lately, or too strong. Think of one moment today when it'll be tested, a meeting, a dinner, a drive, and picture meeting it with that quality a little more refined. Just a little.
Sefirah. Counting: the forty-nine days of the Omer, and for the mystics, one quality refined each day. Today's word.
Your line: refine one quality. Forty-nine nights, one square at a time. That's day six hundred eighty-four.

685.title: Lag BaOmer
685.hook: the thirty-third day breaks the mourning with bonfires, linked to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
685.howItsDone: On Lag BaOmer, the thirty-third day of the Omer, the season's mourning customs are lifted: weddings and haircuts resume, bonfires are lit, especially in Israel, and crowds make pilgrimage to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's tomb in Meron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sefirah, the counting of the Omer, one quality a day. Your line was refine one quality. Today, the thirty-third night of the count.

For weeks, the season has been quiet. In many communities, there have been no weddings, no live music, no haircuts, and people look a little shaggy. Then, on one night in late spring, all over Israel, the sky fills with smoke. Kids have collected scrap wood for days: pallets, old doors, fruit crates. Bonfires burn in parks and empty lots, and families roast potatoes in the coals. In the north, huge crowds pour into a small town to sing and dance around a tomb. The next morning, the barbers are busy and the wedding halls are full.
screen: `WEEKS WITHOUT WEDDINGS OR MUSIC.` → `BONFIRES ALL OVER THE COUNTRY.` → `A CROWD AT A TOMB.`

segments.voice: Lag BaOmer means the thirty-third of the Omer. Hebrew letters are also numbers: lamed is thirty, gimel is three, and together they're said lag. On this day the Omer's mourning customs, which come tomorrow, are lifted. Why the thirty-third? Honestly, the reasons came after the custom. A tradition from the Middle Ages says a plague among Rabbi Akiva's students stopped that day. A later tradition, from the mystics of Safed, says it's the anniversary of the death of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, one of Akiva's students. The Talmud tells his story. He criticized the Roman rulers, was sentenced to death, and hid with his son in a cave for twelve years. A carob tree and a spring appeared to keep them alive, and they studied all day, buried in sand up to their necks to save their clothes. Tradition credits him with the Zohar, a foundational book of Kabbalah; modern historians argue it was written much later, in medieval Spain, and traditional readers keep the older attribution. Both views are held today. The mystics taught that on the day he died, he revealed his deepest secrets and the house filled with light. So a death day became a hilula, the wedding-feast of a soul, and the bonfires are said to recall his light. His tomb is in Meron, in the Galilee, which is why the crowds go there. In some communities, children get their first haircut there, and play with bows and arrows. After weeks of quiet, a break in the sadness.
screen: `LAMED-GIMEL: THIRTY-THREE.` · `REASONS CAME AFTER THE CUSTOM.` · `TWELVE YEARS IN A CAVE.` · `A DEATH DAY TURNED TO LIGHT.` · then, large: `A BREAK IN THE SADNESS.`

segments.voice: If you can, light a candle, safely, or sit by a fireplace, or just watch a flame on a screen. Think of a long stretch that's been heavy for you or someone close, and let this one minute be a break in it: warmth, light, nothing to fix.

686.title: Why the Omer mourns (Yevamot 62b)
686.hook: the Talmud says Akiva's students died in these weeks for not honoring each other
686.howItsDone: During part of the Omer period, many Jews refrain from weddings, haircuts and live music in mourning for Rabbi Akiva's students; Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities count the mourning days differently, and many lift the customs on Lag BaOmer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lag BaOmer, bonfires and Rabbi Shimon. Your line was a break in the sadness. Today, the sadness itself: why these weeks mourn at all.

Twelve thousand pairs of students. That's the number the Talmud gives for the disciples of Rabbi Akiva, spread across the land from Gevat to Antipatris. A whole generation of learners, studying in pairs, arguing over the words of the Torah. If any group seemed set to carry the tradition forward, it was this one. And according to the Talmud, in a single season, all of them died. Its explanation isn't war, or a lack of learning. It's how they treated each other.
screen: `A WHOLE GENERATION OF LEARNERS.` → `GONE IN ONE SEASON.` → `HOW THEY TREATED EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: The passage is in tractate Yevamot, page 62b. Twelve thousand pairs means twenty-four thousand students, and all of them died in one period, because they did not treat each other with respect. They died, it adds, between Passover and Shavuot, and the world was desolate. Then Akiva went south and taught just five new students, among them Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, from yesterday. Those five carried the Torah forward. Now the irony. Rabbi Akiva is the one who called a verse from Leviticus, in the old Jewish translation, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," a great principle of the Torah. In the Talmud's account, his own students fell short of that very teaching. They knew the texts; they didn't honor the people learning beside them. Some historians suggest the deaths may also reflect the Bar Kokhba revolt against Rome, in which Akiva supported the rebels; the Talmud doesn't say so. Either way, the rabbis chose to remember it as a lesson about respect. That's why, in many communities, these weeks carry quiet mourning for part of the Omer: no weddings, no haircuts, no live music. Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities count the mourning days differently. And some teachers turn the mourning into a task: if the students died for lack of honoring each other, the repair is to honor each other more, especially the people you argue with.
screen: `TWELVE THOUSAND PAIRS.` · `NO RESPECT FOR EACH OTHER.` · `FIVE STUDENTS IN THE SOUTH.` · `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR, AKIVA TAUGHT.` · then, large: `HONOR EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you work, study or live beside, especially someone you disagree with, compete with, or take for granted, and picture their face. Name one thing about them that deserves honor, their effort, their honesty, their patience, a skill you don't have, and hold it until it feels true.
Rabbi Akiva, whose twenty-four thousand students all died in one season, the Talmud says, because they did not treat each other with respect.
Your line: honor each other. A week of enough, as if you left, an open door, a song of songs, one quality, a break in the sadness, and now honor. Day six hundred eighty-six, done.
